To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
dosage-balance stabilizing selection slows the rate of compensatory drift and can facilitate neofunctionalizing mutations.

compensatory drift can cause the expression of duplicate genes to diverge from the optimum even when dosage-balance selection is strong, but the rate of divergence decreases with the strength of selection, the size and the size of the effect of mutations, and with population size.

even under strong dosage-balance constraints, duplicate genes can diverge by compensatory drift and that compensatory drift can impede neofunctionalizing mutations early after duplication but later can facilitate neofunctionalizations.

dosage-balance can facilitate the fixation of neofunctionalizations but only after the paralogs have drifted apart.
dosage-balance is a powerful force that constrains the evolution of paralogs, and that it can also facilitate the evolution of paralog function.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
dosage-balance is not a strong barrier to neofunctionalize, but that it does impede neofunctionalizing mutations in early stages of evolution after a duplication.
compensatory drift may be an important factor in the evolution of dosage-balanced genes, and dosage-balance selection is a key factor in determining the dynamics of duplicate-gene evolution.

The main takeaway from our work is that
dosage-balance stabilizing selection is a powerful force for the preservation of duplicate genes and that it can also facilitate the evolution of new functions.
compensatory drift may be an important evolutionary process for the evolution of gene expression levels and gene functions.

the evolutionary dynamics of dosage-sensitive duplicates are not simply a tug-of-war between dosage-balance and stabilizing selection, and dosage-balance selection can facilitate, rather than inhibit, the evolution of neofunctionalizing duplicates.
